1070:
A. Mayor and Council shall oversee upcoming Corridor Map and Standards, and shall continually guide Corridor development.
B. Corridor Design shall be considered a part of the planning functions of the City.
C. Mayor and Council, themselves functioning as the body to oversee Corridor Design, shall:
1) Preserve and improve integrity, aesthetics, livability and safety of the Corridors;
2) Review applications for Certificates of Appropriateness.
3) Make such investigations and studies of matters relating to as they deem necessary or appropriate for the purpose of maximizing the appropriate use, preservation, development and utility of the Corridors.
D. Mayor and Council shall follow Zoning Procedures Law (ZPL) and may adopt rules for Designation, Standards, and consideration of applications, via amendment to this Ordinance. All building permits in the Corridors shall come before Mayor and Council for consideration.
E. The following design language shall outline Council's intent until standards are adopted; once adopted, standards shall prevail if language conflicts:
A variety of architectural styles exist in the city - these standards do not prescribe any one style as most appropriate. Our neighborhoods represent a broad range of styles typical of the 19th century through the present, with no single style predominant. New residences may use a style appropriate to the intended use and the context of the surrounding area. Design may use contemporary materials to adapt historic design elements into a new residence.
In terms of site planning and massing, applicants shall follow the City zoning, but homes facing the street should generally be designed with setbacks similar to other traditional homes on the subject Corridor. New single-family homes should be on an appropriate scale consistent with nearby historical and/or traditional building construction types. Home height and square footage on the Corridors should be harmonious and consistent with other nearby traditional homes on the Corridors, Homes should not be more than 15 percent smaller than the smallest home on the Corridor in which they are being planned, nor more than 15 percent larger by heated square footage than the largest existing home on that Corridor. If multiple homes are being built at the same time or nearby, they should not be the same design or plan, nor a 'flipped' or slightly modified version of a nearby plan. Turn and deceleration lanes will generally not be required on Corridors. Homes on lots that face a city street shall face the street, and front-facing garages are not allowed per Zoning. If homes within 400 feet on the corridor are historical in nature (built prior to 1940), then new homes should also reflect the historic nature of those homes.
Should the nearby homes on a particular Corridor in question not be reflective of current market trends, be inconsistent with traditional homes on the Corridors generally, and/or not be subject to a zoning overlay, architect, draftsman or builder is required to reflect, with architectural details, fenestration and trim work details, the style and design of historic homes published on pages 1-35 in "Vintage Houses in Oconee" written by Albert Wimpy Ward and Susan McCreery LaCount. These homes typify the longstanding pattern of traditional and historic development in our small town and others nearby that contributes to the attractiveness of our gateway entry corridors.
New construction should adhere to existing nearby development patterns for the purpose of retaining and enhancing the aesthetic qualities of the area, with an emphasis on residential construction being complementary of and consistent with existing nearby residential dwellings or the historic character of Watkinsville. A residence whose form and architecture are high quality contributes to the character of the neighborhood. Residences should be constructed of high quality, long-lasting materials to contribute to the city's stability, character and pedestrian experience. Materials should be compatible with existing and/or desired context of nearby areas and common to the area's historic construction methods/style. High-quality materials result in residences as maintenance free as possible. Materials should be consistent with and relate to architectural style of the residence and appropriate to the scale. This may include contemporary materials adapted to historic design elements. Important character defining details such as brick patterns, joint spacing and color should be incorporated. Exteriors should reflect and complement the traditional materials and design of our historic and traditional architecture. They should express construction techniques and structural constraints of traditional, long-lasting materials. Simple configurations and solid craftsmanship are favored over complexity and ostentation in form and details.
The following are encouraged: Brick, Native stone (or synthetic equivalent), Pre-cast masonry (for trim and cornice elements only), Gypsum Reinforced Fiber Concrete (GRFC - for trim elements only), Metal (for beams, lintels, trim elements and ornamentation only), Split-faced block (only for piers, foundation walls, and chimneys), Wood lap siding, Hardie-Plank™ equivalent or better siding. Homes should show a consistent use of materials and design on all sides (no brick front with Hardie-Plank™ sides and rear, for example). Chimneys should be brick, stone or masonry elements.

(Ord. of 4-17-2024, § II)

1072:
A. If a property is in the Corridors, no Material Change in Appearance of such property, or of a structure, in the Corridors, shall be made, until a Certificate of Appropriateness has been approved. Modifications to 1) homes, or to 2) approved COA's, which are in either case minor, that do not constitute a Material Change in Appearance, qualify for an expedited, Administrative, review. Requests shall be accompanied by professional quality or functional equivalent elevations, drawings, photos and plans that describe such. Administrative review shall be for work which constitutes a minor modification which clearly and distinctly complies with established criteria and standards. Administrative review decisions shall be reported to the Council at the next meeting.
B. The Council may issue a Certificate of Appropriateness to new structures in the Corridors, which shall conform in design, scale and setback, to the requirements in forthcoming Standards to be advertised and approved in compliance with the ZPL.
C. Thirty days prior to submitting a final plan, a Conceptual Design Review should occur. Conceptual Design Review has two objectives: (1) early input with reduced design investment; and (2) design framework formation. It provides potential development applicants, property owners, and Mayor and/or City staff a process and venue to exchange design ideas during early project development. The setting is informal to ease collaboration and idea exchange of fundamental, design framework components. The end product is consensus direction. Staff will provide advisories to the potential development applicant. The applicant's builder, architect, engineer or draftsman should attend. This informal courtesy consultation with mayor and/or staff is possible at least 15 days prior to application for COA to help applicants identify issues and options. This process is a preliminary step before formal COA and building permit application and it does not provide complete technical and/or environmental analysis as it may pertain to the City's applicable Community or Master Plan or Specific Plan or Zoning Regulations. Conceptual Design Review applications are opened, processed and closed. Multiple conceptual review applications (separate fee) may be processed at the same time if a builder has multiple homes planned. Proposals for conceptual design review should preferably be emailed, and be accompanied by: 3-D renderings, representative architecture or drawings of homes that are planned (or photos of homes with the same floorplans and similar finish levels); Contextual slides showing other homes on the corridor or in Watkinsville that the design is responsive to; a map of the lot(s) showing general sites of the home(s); elevations, drawings, photos or plans. Any plans should be certified by an architect, draftsman or engineer as complying with (or indicating a commitment to comply with) all City Ordinances and Codes aside from the corridor design standards under discussion.
Comments during a review are non-binding first-impressions to assist applicant in refining the project. Comments are based on concepts and limited information and subject to change. Common agenda items may include: Clarification on how project can comply; Discussion of circumstances preventing applicant from meeting the standards. Any changes may result in reconsideration of the informal comments provided. Depending on complexity, staff may require additional time to research. Staff is not responsible for identifying all possible issues or specifically suggesting design approaches or alternatives.
D. Acceptable Reaction to Applications for Certificate of Appropriateness.
1) Mayor and Council shall issue a Certificate of Appropriateness if it finds the proposed change(s) would not have a substantial adverse effect on the Corridors. Mayor and Council shall consider, in addition to any other pertinent factors, consistency with the pattern of traditional and historic development nearby, architectural value and significance, architectural style, general design arrangement, texture, and material of the architectural features, and the relationship thereof to the exterior architectural style, and features of the other structures in the neighborhood.
2) Table/withdrawal. If Mayor and Council are unable to decide because the application is insufficient, it shall be treated as incomplete. If Mayor and Council are unable to decide because the applicant or representative is unavailable, they may deny, or table to a date certain no later than the next regularly scheduled meeting. The time to decide an application before it is deemed approved shall be tolled if tabling is due to applicant's unavailability.
3) If Mayor and Council identify elements not in compliance with the and the proposal would have a substantial adverse effect on the Corridor, they may recommend changes to render the application compliant. If applicant agrees, Mayor and Council shall, conditioned upon the changes being memorialized in revised plans, approve the application as so modified and issue a COA after the decision.
4) Mayor and Council shall deny a Certificate, if it finds the Material Change in Appearance would have substantial adverse effects on the Corridor or structure(s) therein, and shall state its reasons, and may suggest alternative courses of action, which may facilitate a compliant future application for a COA. The applicant may modify plans and resubmit the application at any time.
[E. Reserved.]
F. 15—45 days prior to review of an application, the City shall run an ad in the legal organ and post a sign, and shall give applicant and such owners and other citizens an opportunity to be heard. It shall be a 11" × 17" or larger sign in a conspicuous place on the property. The sign shall read generally: "An application has been filed with the City regarding this property, requesting a Certificate of Appropriateness to allow the following work: _______. A public hearing will be held by the Mayor and Council to review and decide the matter at City Hall, Watkinsville, Georgia, on [DATE], at [TIME]. All persons having an interest in this application should be at this hearing to voice interest. Visit City Hall or Call 706-769-5161 for details."
Procedure: Speakers should provide supporting documentation prior to date of hearing. Speakers shall sign the speaker list. Property owner and/or applicant and the public shall have no less than 10 minutes per side, with equal time to both the 1) owner/applicant/supporters and 2) opponents. Once the hearing ends, only Mayor and Council and staff speak, unless questions are posed.
G. In its review of applications, Mayor and Council shall not consider interior arrangement or use having no effect on exterior architectural features, safety or utility.
H. Mayor and Council shall approve or reject within 45 days after filing thereof. Failure to act within 45 days shall constitute approval, and no other evidence of approval shall be needed.
I. If Mayor and Council reject an application, it shall state reasons, and transmit a record, in writing, to applicant. Mayor and Council may suggest alternatives. Applicant may make modifications and resubmit. If the application covers a change which would require a building permit, rejection shall be binding on the officer charged with issuing building permits and, in such case, no building permit shall be issued.
J. Work not per a Certificate of Appropriateness is prohibited.
K. A Certificate of Appropriateness shall become void unless construction is commenced within 6 months. Certificates shall be issued for 18 months, at which time they shall expire. A new application must be made and a new Certificate obtained for any construction or other modification after 18 months from the original Certificate.
(Ord. of 4-17-2024, § IV)
1073:
A. Mayor and Council have authority over any request to demolish or relocate a structure in the Corridors.
B. A public meeting shall be scheduled for each application for demolition prior to the 30-day delay period specified below.
C. Mayor and Council shall not approve a demolition request without reviewing at the same time the plans for the building that would replace the structure. If a building constructed prior to 1940 or one that is designated historic is demolished, preference will be given to new construction that reflects historic architecture in Watkinsville.
D. Criteria. If a property owner shows a building is incapable of an economic return on its value, as appraised, and Mayor and Council fail to issue a Certificate of Appropriateness, such may be demolished; provided, however, for buildings constructed prior to 1940, before a demolition permit is issued, 30 days' notice of proposed demolition shall be given. Notice shall be posted on the premises in a location clearly visible from the street to give persons, societies, or organizations the opportunity to acquire or arrange for preservation of such buildings.
(Ord. of 4-17-2024, § V)
1074:
A. Ordinary maintenance or repair required to prevent deterioration of the property does not require a COA and is excluded from any review hereunder. Ordinary maintenance or repair is to correct deterioration, decay or damage, or to sustain the existing form, and does not involve a change in exterior appearance. Owners shall not allow structures to deteriorate by failure of maintenance and repair. Such failure is a violation and adversely impacts the value of the Corridors, and jeopardizes structural integrity and poses hazards. All properties and structures in Corridors shall be kept free from structural defects and conditions.
B. Nothing in this Ordinance shall be construed as to exempt property owners from complying with existing City codes, nor to prevent any property owner from making any use of his property not prohibited by other statutes, ordinances, or regulations.
(Ord. of 4-17-2024, § VI)

1078:
a) "Certificate of Appropriateness" - a document approving a proposal to make a material change in the appearance of a property or of a structure or site in the Corridors, which must be obtained from Mayor and Council before such material change may be undertaken.
b) "Exterior architectural features" - the architectural style, general design, and general arrangement of the exterior of a building or structure, including the kind of texture of the building material; the type and style of all windows, doors, and signs; and other appurtenant architectural fixtures, features, details, or elements relative to the foregoing.
c) "Material Change in Appearance" - a change that will affect only the exterior architectural features of a property or of any structure in the Corridors and may include any of the following:
1) Reconstruction or alteration of size, shape, or facade, including relocation of doors or windows or removal or alteration of any architectural features, details, or elements;
2) Demolition;
3) Commencement of excavation;
4) A change in location of advertising visible from the public way; or
5) Construction, alteration, restoration, or removal of any structure in the Corridors.
(Ord. of 4-17-2024, § X)

A variety of architectural styles exist in the city - these standards do not prescribe any one style as most appropriate. Our neighborhoods represent a broad range of styles typical of the 19th century through the present, with no single style predominant. New residences may use a style appropriate to the intended use and the context of the surrounding area. Design may use contemporary materials to adapt historic design elements into a new residence.
Designs submitted by applicants and the proposed architectural elements such as window mullions, shutters, masonry, exterior veneers, cornice detailing and window casing, should demonstrate consistency with traditional architectural designs of the Corridors, be harmonious with the scenic qualities representative of the city's historic character, achieve a standard for design in the Corridors, and have quality similar to other homes on the Corridors.
These standards achieve quality contextual design, encourage reasonable diversity of styles, provide design flexibility instead of aesthetic control, improve property values, and provide investor and property owner confidence through architectural continuity. Architecture refers to relationship and culmination of features of a building including texture, proportion, entrance, doors, windows, trim, roof, materials and color, in addition to mass and scale. A residence whose form and architecture are high quality contributes to the character of the neighborhood.
Height and square footage should be harmonious and consistent with other nearby traditional homes. Should the nearby homes not be reflective of current market trends, be inconsistent with traditional homes on the Corridors, and/or not be subject to a zoning overlay, architect or builder is encouraged to reflect, with architectural details, fenestration and trim work details, the style and design of historic homes on pages 1-35 in "Vintage Houses in Oconee" by Ward and LaCount. These typify the longstanding pattern of traditional and historic development in our small town that contributes to the attractiveness of our gateway entry corridors. New construction should adhere to existing nearby development patterns for retaining and enhancing the aesthetic qualities of the area, with an emphasis on residential construction being complementary of and consistent with existing nearby residential dwellings.
The design of the front is critical for the atmosphere along the street. Front facades contribute to a unified streetscape creating a sense of place. Facades shall be parallel to the street. The front is the most highly designed side utilizing the following elements: A change in plane, building wall projection or recess; high Architectural details; Variety in material and texture; often a Porch; Shutters; entrance emphasized by a gable or stoop; and Arches, columns, cornices.
Residences should be constructed of high quality, long-lasting materials to contribute to the city's stability, character and pedestrian experience. Materials should be compatible with the existing and/or desired context of nearby areas and common to the area's historic construction methods/style. High-quality materials result in residences as maintenance free as possible. Materials should be consistent with and relate to the architectural style of the residence and appropriate to the scale. This may include contemporary materials adapted to historic design elements. Important character defining details such as brick patterns, joint spacing and color should be incorporated. Exteriors should reflect and complement the traditional materials and design of our historic and traditional architecture. They should express the construction techniques and structural constraints of traditional, long-lasting materials. Simple configurations and solid craftsmanship are favored over complexity and ostentation in form and details.
The following are encouraged: Brick, Native stone (or synthetic equivalent), Pre-cast masonry (for trim and cornice elements only), Gypsum Reinforced Fiber Concrete (GRFC-for trim elements only), Metal (for beams, lintels, trim elements and ornamentation only), Split-faced block (only for piers, foundation walls, and chimneys), Wood lap siding, Hardie-Plank™ equivalent or better siding.
Roofs are one of the most highly visible components - they contribute to and are integral to overall design through distinctive, defined styles and decorative patterns and colors. They should be consistent with the style of the residence utilizing architectural elements such as cornice treatments, roof overhangs with brackets, and richly textured materials. Roofs and parapets shall utilize appropriate pitch, drainage, and materials to provide visual coherence in the Corridor. The following are encouraged: Shingles - Asphalt or Metal (dimensional type); Metal - galvanized steel, copper, aluminum, or zinc-alum. Down spouts must match gutters in material and finish, unless rain chains or another feature is utilized.
Windows are a vital element, which link the private (space within a residence) and public realms. Doors are also a vital element providing not only visual but, physical connections between the public and private realms. Windows shall be appropriately sized for the residence, and typically divided by multiple panes of glass to help the window "hold" the surface of the facade, rather than appearing like a "hole" in the wall via a large single sheet of glass. Shaped Frames and Sills should be used to enhance openings and add additional relief and be proportional to the glass area framed; e.g. a larger window should have thicker framing.
The following are encouraged - anodized aluminum, wood, clad wood, vinyl, or steel. Exterior shutters, if applied, should be sized and mounted appropriately for the window (one-half the width), even if inoperable.
Doors- Doors should enhance and support the architectural style. Doors with transoms are encouraged when appropriate for the style of the residence Doors should be solid and well detailed. They should match the materials, design and character of the front facade window framing.
In terms of site planning and massing, applicants shall follow City zoning, but homes facing the street should generally be designed with setbacks similar to other traditional homes on the subject Corridor. New single-family homes should be on an appropriate scale consistent with nearby historical and/or traditional building construction types and generally not be more than 15 percent smaller than the smallest home on the Corridor in which they are being planned, nor typically more than 15 percent larger by heated square footage than the largest existing home on that Corridor. If multiple homes are built at the same time or nearby, they typically should not be the same design or plan, nor a 'flipped' or slightly modified version of a nearby plan.
Vehicle storage, garbage and mechanical equipment should not be visible from the street. Garages shall be 200 - 400 square feet, and are to be enclosed with overheard doors. Detached garages should be constructed in the same architectural style, colors and materials as the dwelling. Car ports built of wood and matching the architectural style of the home may be considered if consistent with historic design along the corridor. Sidewalks will be installed if shown on the City's future transportation plan. Per city code, slab construction is not allowed.
